headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: nullclaw’s broad filesystem/network/MCP access can collide with AutoGPT’s shell/filesystem autonomy.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGPT can read and act on filesystem content, while nullclaw exposes workspace files, web channels, and MCP-style delegation. That creates a plausible instruction-injection path if nullclaw forwards untrusted content into AutoGPT’s inputs. The pairwise bridge is documented by both profiles, though no direct exploit evidence is provided.
conditions: IF nullclaw passes workspace or webhook content into AutoGPT prompts without sanitization
IF AutoGPT treats file or API content as instructions rather than data
mitigations: Add a strict content/instruction separator in the handoff
Disable automatic prompt ingestion from shared files
Require human review before delegating web or MCP content
Use allowlisted templates for any cross-agent messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: Nullclaw explicitly handles secrets, conversation history, audit logs, and workspace files, and it has broad network egress plus file read/write. AutoGPT has filesystem access and allowlisted egress, so sensitive material can move from nullclaw’s workspace into AutoGPT outputs or external calls. The default pair therefore risks exfiltration or unintended disclosure.
conditions: IF nullclaw stores secrets or conversation history in its workspace
IF AutoGPT reads those files and forwards derived content through its allowlisted egress
mitigations: Separate workspaces for each agent
Remove secrets from shared directories
Block AutoGPT from reading nullclaw secret-bearing paths
Turn off outbound calls for any task touching sensitive files
Rotate any credentials already placed in shared storage

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands and access files; nullclaw can also modify git state and write the filesystem, while AutoGPT can spawn subprocesses and use the filesystem. With no locking or coordination primitive shown, concurrent writes to shared paths or git state can corrupt work or overwrite each other.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory or git repository
IF either agent writes while the other is reading or committing
mitigations: Assign distinct working directories
Serialize git operations with a lock file
Disable one agent’s write access during the other’s run
Use read-only mounts for shared inputs
Snapshot the workspace before concurrent tasks

D_cascading_error.rationale: Nullclaw’s outputs can flow through webhooks, agent-card, or delegation channels, and AutoGPT can consume files and act via shell. That makes it plausible for one agent’s unverified output to become the other’s operational input. The pair is not inherently self-verifying, so errors can cascade across work products.
conditions: IF AutoGPT consumes nullclaw-generated files, webhooks, or agent-card content as authoritative
IF no verification step checks facts before shell or API actions
mitigations: Insert a verification step before any action-taking
Require citations or source links for transferred facts
Limit nullclaw outputs to structured, typed fields
Have a human approve high-impact actions
Log and diff all cross-agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: Nullclaw explicitly touches audit logs, conversation history, workspace files, and secrets, while AutoGPT can access files and network egress. If regulated data is placed into nullclaw’s workspace and then processed by AutoGPT, retention or residency obligations may diverge. The profiles do not specify certifications, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated data such as customer records or secrets is stored in nullclaw’s workspace
IF AutoGPT processes or transmits that data outside the required residency or retention boundary
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Document retention and deletion rules for both agents
Restrict outbound destinations for regulated tasks
Use separate tenants or accounts for each agent
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
